 - A coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) is an operation to improve blood flow to your heart. It involves using healthy blood vessels taken from another part of your body to get round (bypass) a narrowed or blocked artery. It's also sometimes called heart bypass surgery. It's done to treat coronary heart disease, where the arteries that supply blood to your heart (coronary arteries) become blocked or too narrow. A coronary artery bypass graft treats symptoms of coronary heart disease such as chest pain (angina) and helps to prevent heart attacks.  - Coronary angioplasty is also known as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or balloon angioplasty. During the procedure, a small balloon is inserted to push the fatty tissue in the narrowed artery outwards. A metal stent (a wire mesh tube) is usually placed in the artery to hold it open. 
 - Some patients after a stent also take an anticoagulant — bleeding risk is higher. Report any bleeding promptly and do not stop medicines without advice. 
 - Taking clopidogrel helps prevent blood clots if you have an increased risk of having them. Your risk is higher if you have or have had: - a heart attack - unstable angina - a stroke or "mini-stroke" (transient ischaemic attack or TIA) - peripheral arterial disease - atrial fibrillation - an operation on your heart or blood vessels, such as a coronary stent insertion Clopidogrel is only available on prescription. It comes as tablets.

cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - You can wait for now. It's important you get medical attention immediately if you think you might have a heart attack. 
 - You can sit down and stay calm. Don't worry about wasting anyone's time. 
 - You can take 300mg aspirin if you have it and you're not allergic. It's important you get medical attention immediately. 
  
 When to get help: 
 - If you think you might have a heart attack, call 999 immediately. It's important you get medical attention immediately. 
  
 Source note: [BHF Heart attack] You should call 999 for an ambulance if you think you might have a heart attack. [University Hospital Southampton cardiac surgery PDF] Generally, you should wait 12 weeks to swim and be more active on holiday. [Coronary angioplasty and stents (PCI)] You should not drive for at least a week after having an angioplasty and stent — longer if you also had a heart attack. [NHS Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) for angina] You should sit down and rest. Use one spray under your tongue or one tablet under your tongue if prescribed tablets. Wait 5 minutes. If pain is not relieved, use a second dose. Wait another 5 minutes. If pain is still not relieved after two doses, call 999 immediately — this may be a heart attack, not angina. [NHS Deep vein thrombosis DVT] If you think you have DVT, you can call 111 or get help from 111 online. If you're pregnant, you can also call an early pregnancy unit or your maternity unit.

cases.prompt: I had a heart attack recently. It's been 35 weeks since my event. What are common side effects of beta blockers?
cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - Beta blockers are common after a heart attack to help your heart and blood vessels. 
 - They can make you feel tired, dizzy, or have trouble sleeping. 
 - If these side effects are bad, tell your doctor right away. 
  
 When to get help: 
 - If you have shortness of breath, wheezing, or chest tightness, it could be a sign of lung problems. 
 - If you have yellowish skin or yellow eyes, it could be a sign of liver problems. 
 - If you have any other unusual symptoms, tell your doctor. 
  
 Source note: 
 The information is from the NHS and St George's medications after acute coronary syndrome PDF. It covers common side effects of beta blockers, including tiredness, dizziness, and cold hands and feet.

 - It's important to set achievable goals for your recovery, and progress may be slow but every small improvement builds confidence.

 - Emotional recovery can take time, so it's important to accept what has happened and find ways of living in peace with it.

 - Call 999 in an emergency if you have any symptoms that are severe or life-threatening.

cases.prompt: Please be specific to my heart recovery. I'm 33 weeks into recovery. I had a heart attack recently. I feel panicky whenever I notice my heartbeat.
cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - If you feel panicky about your heartbeat, try to stay calm and breathe slowly. 
 - If you feel very worried, call 999 for an ambulance right away. 
  
 When to get help: 
 - If you feel very worried or panicky, call 999 for an ambulance right away. 
  
 Source note: 
 - [BHF Heart attack] You should call 999 for an ambulance if you feel very worried or panicky. 
 - [Coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG)] All types of surgery come with risk. With heart bypass surgery, the risks can include an irregular heartbeat, bleeding, blood clots, failure of the graft to work as well as it should, complications after surgery like a heart attack or stroke, general anaesthesia effects: short-term confusion, lack of concentration, sickness and dizziness, wound infection. 
 - [NHS Recovering from a heart attack] Heart attacks affect people in different ways. For some, it may take several weeks to recover, but there will be little impact on their life. For others, recovery can take months or years. After having a heart attack, you'll usually need to rest, including taking time off work, be referred to cardiac rehabilitation to help with your recovery – this may involve attending appointments in-person, or taking part remotely from home using video calls or apps, Most people can continue with their normal activities once they've recovered. You may feel anxious or worried about getting back to your usual tasks or going back to work. Talk to your GP if you're feeling anxious or you have low mood after having a heart attack. They can help you get support. 
 - [Guy's and St Thomas' after coronary angioplasty] If you have recently had a heart attack, talk to your doctor or nurse about returning to work and driving — you will likely need to wait. Return to work: usually within 1 week, unless manual job involving heavy lifting Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous exercise for at least 5 days Driving: Not allowed for 1 week after coronary angioplasty (DVLA requirement). Contact the DVLA if you have an HGV or PSV licence Check with your insurance company. Flying: Usually safe 1 to 2 weeks after the procedure — check with your airline and insurance Other activities (including sex): can be resumed when you feel ready

cases.prompt: Can this wait, or do I need advice today? I'm 33 weeks into recovery. I had a heart attack recently. I feel panicky whenever I notice my heartbeat.
cases.patient_answer:
About your question ("Original concern: Can this wait, or do I need advice today? I'm 33 weeks…"): Here is approved recovery information that may help: 
  
 - You should: - call 999 for an ambulance - sit down and stay calm - take 300mg aspirin if you have it and you're not allergic - wait for the ambulance It's important you get medical attention immediately. Do not worry about wasting anyone's time. A heart attack is a medical emergency. 
 - Wait a few weeks, until you've started cardiac rehabilitation and can be assessed by a professional. If you have had prompt treatment after a heart attack, you may quickly feel better physically but it is still best to let the heart recover. Do not do any sport without seeking the advice of a professional first. 
 - If you have recently had a heart attack, talk to your doctor or nurse about returning to work and driving — you will likely need to wait. - Return to work: usually within 1 week, unless manual job involving heavy lifting - Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous exercise for at least 5 days - Driving: Not allowed for 1 week after coronary angioplasty (DVLA requirement). Contact the DVLA if you have an HGV or PSV licence. Check with your insurance company. - Flying: Usually safe 1 to 2 weeks after the procedure — check with your airline and insurance - Other activities (including sex): can be resumed when you feel ready 
  
 What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed. 
  
 When to get help: if your symptoms get worse, or you feel more unwell or worried, contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111. Call 999 in an emergency. 
  
 Source note: this information is drawn from the approved sources listed above.

 - A coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) is an operation to improve blood flow to your heart. It involves using healthy blood vessels taken from another part of your body to get round (bypass) a narrowed or blocked artery. It's also sometimes called heart bypass surgery. It's done to treat coronary heart disease, where the arteries that supply blood to your heart (coronary arteries) become blocked or too narrow. A coronary artery bypass graft treats symptoms of coronary heart disease such as chest pain (angina) and helps to prevent heart attacks. Most people need treatment for 3 arteries (called a triple bypass) or 4 arteries (a quadruple bypass). Some people only need treatment for 1 or 2 arteries (a single or double bypass).  - You can eat a healthy diet and exercise as advised by your doctor. 
 - You can avoid smoking and limit alcohol. 
 - You can keep your blood pressure and cholesterol levels under control. 
 - You can avoid stress and get enough rest. 
 - You can contact your cardiac team if you have any concerns or symptoms. 
  
 When to get help: 
 - If you have any new or worsening symptoms, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling in your legs. 
 - If you have any signs of infection, such as fever or chills.

You asked about tiredness. Here is approved recovery information that may help: 
  
 - Coming to terms with a long-term condition such as heart disease can put a strain on you, your family and your friends. 
 - Page updated: 15 June 2022 When you're recovering from a heart attack, stroke, surgery or illness, getting back on your feet can take time. 
 - Finding that you can't do all the things you used to do is very common and can feel frustrating. You may need to re-learn daily activities like bathing, cooking, or dressing. Recovery is an active, dynamic process. It isn't just "rest, rest, rest". It's also gently pushing at the limits of what's comfortable in terms of exercise and activity. Try to do a little more each day or each week, but don't overdo it. Pacing — staying within your limits without getting exhausted — is important to avoid a cycle of "boom and bust". The risk is that you feel slightly better, try to go back to normal, and quickly feel exhausted, which sets you further back. Pacing is especially important if you feel breathless or tired (e.g., if you have heart failure, or post-viral fatigue).

It involves using healthy blood vessels taken from another part of your body to get round (bypass) a narrowed or blocked artery. It's also sometimes called heart bypass surgery. A coronary artery bypass graft treats symptoms of coronary heart disease such as chest pain (angina) and helps to prevent heart attacks. Most people need treatment for 3 arteries (called a triple bypass) or 4 arteries (a quadruple bypass). Some people only need treatment for 1 or 2 arteries (a single or double bypass). You'll be given local anaesthetic at the start of the procedure. A narrow flexible tube (called a catheter) is put into your wrist or groin and pushed up to the coronary artery. A small balloon at the end of the tube is blown up to widen the narrowed part of your artery.  - Coronary bypass surgery is a type of surgery where 'bypasses' are created around narrowings or blockages in the arteries of your heart, to help bring back blood supply to it. When you have a blocked or narrow artery around your heart, coronary bypass surgery creates a new route for blood to flow to your heart muscle. A healthy vessel from your chest or leg is removed and reused as a new path around your heart. You might be recommended surgery if your arteries cannot be treated with coronary angioplasty or stenting. You may also be offered surgery if multiple arteries are affected, or you have other problems with your blood vessels.

A small balloon at the end of the tube is blown up to widen the narrowed part of your artery. Sometimes if the artery is so narrow that the balloon cannot pass through it, a tiny drill might also be used (this is called rotablation) to chip away at the fatty deposits and gradually widen the narrowing.  - Coronary bypass surgery is a type of surgery where 'bypasses' are created around narrowings or blockages in the arteries of your heart, to help bring back blood supply to it. When you have a blocked or narrow artery around your heart, coronary bypass surgery creates a new route for blood to flow to your heart muscle. A healthy vessel from your chest or leg is removed and reused as a new path around your heart. You might be recommended surgery if your arteries cannot be treated with coronary angioplasty or stenting. You may also be offered surgery if multiple arteries are affected, or you have other problems with your blood vessels.

cases.prompt: I had open-heart bypass surgery recently. I'm 52 weeks past my procedure. When can I lift things after angioplasty?
cases.patient_answer:
Follow your clinical team's activity guidance. Do not exceed limits in your discharge letter. 
  
 About your question ("Original concern: I had open-heart bypass surgery recently. I'm 52 weeks…"): Here is approved recovery information that may help: 
  
 - Page updated: 12 August 2025 | Next review: 12 August 2028 Coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG), also known as heart bypass surgery, is a procedure that treats coronary heart disease. It is sometimes pronounced like 'cabbage'. 
 - Emergency treatment may include: - Coronary angioplasty — putting one or more stents into the narrowed or blocked artery to keep it open and improve blood supply to the heart - Thrombolysis — "clot-busting" medicine to dissolve the blood clot blocking the coronary artery - Coronary bypass surgery — attaching a blood vessel from your leg, arm or chest in your heart to go around the blocked artery 
 - Coronary bypass surgery is a type of surgery where 'bypasses' are created around narrowings or blockages in the arteries of your heart, to help bring back blood supply to it. When you have a blocked or narrow artery around your heart, coronary bypass surgery creates a new route for blood to flow to your heart muscle. A healthy vessel from your chest or leg is removed and reused as a new path around your heart. You might be recommended surgery if your arteries cannot be treated with coronary angioplasty or stenting. You may also be offered surgery if multiple arteries are affected, or you have other problems with your blood vessels. 
  
 What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed. 
  
 When to get help: if your symptoms get worse, or you feel more unwell or worried, contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111. Call 999 in an emergency.

cases.patient_answer:
About your question ("Original concern: What happens at cardiac rehabilitation? (For context:…"): Here is approved recovery information that may help:

 - After your coronary angioplasty, you are looked after in the recovery unit before being transferred back to the ward. Pulse and blood pressure are checked and recorded. 
 - Cardiac rehabilitation should be offered if you've had a heart operation. This programme aims to help you recover from the procedure and get back to everyday life as quickly as possible. Your cardiac rehabilitation programme will begin when you're in hospital. You should also be invited back for another session taking place within about 4 to 8 weeks after you leave hospital. A member of the cardiac rehabilitation team will visit you in hospital and provide detailed information about: - your state of health - the type of treatment you received - what medications you'll need when you leave hospital - what specific risk factors are thought to have contributed to needing the operation - what lifestyle changes you can make to address those risk factors 
  
 What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed. 
  
 When to get help: if your symptoms get worse, or you feel more unwell or worried, contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111. Call 999 in an emergency.

cases.prompt: I have limited health literacy. Can my partner come to cardiac rehab with me? (For context: I'm recovering after a cardiac device implant, 17 weeks into recovery.)
cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - Your partner can come to cardiac rehab with you. It's a good idea to have someone with you to help you and support you. 
 - You can join a cardiac rehabilitation program. This is a special program that helps you get back to normal activities and feel better. 
 - Your health care team can help you with this. They know how to make sure you're doing things safely and correctly. 
 - You can start doing things that help you feel better, like taking baths and showers. But you should wait a few days before doing this. 
 - You can go on trips like car rides, trains, or airplanes. But you should tell the people who take care of you about your pacemaker. 
 - You can stay away from things that might hurt your pacemaker, like magnets or strong electrical fields. 
 - You can tell other doctors, nurses, and health care professionals about your pacemaker. They need to know so they can help you. 
 - You can let the TSA know you have a pacemaker when you're at the airport. They might need to do a special check. 
 - You can tell your partner about your pacemaker when you're at the airport. They can help you stay safe. 
 When to get help: 
 - If you have any questions or if you're not sure about something, talk to your health care team. 
 - If you feel any of these things, you should get help right away: 
   - Your pacemaker feels like it's not working right 
   - You have a fever or other sickness 
   - You have any other unusual symptoms 
 - If you feel any of these things, you should call 999 for help. 
 Source note: The information in this answer is based on the British Heart Foundation's BHF Cardiac arrest recovery, Gloucestershire Hospitals cardiology, Guy's and St Thomas' having a pacemaker or ICD fitted, and AHA Living with your pacemaker. cases.prompt: It's been 16 weeks since my event. I'm recovering after heart valve surgery. Something doesn't feel right since this morning.
cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - Keep your upper arms close to your body when moving or lifting, as if in an 'imaginary tube' at the beginning of recovery. 
 - Be guided by your pain level. You can perform mindful movement outside of the tube, including lifting, as long as your pain level doesn't increase. 
 - There are no weight restrictions — you can lift or carry anything providing your pain level doesn't increase. 
  
 When to get help: 
 - If you have any pain or discomfort, or if you feel unwell, contact your cardiac team or GP. 
  
 Source note: 
 The information provided is based on the guidelines and advice given by the Royal Papworth Hospital, which is recognized as one of the leading centres for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).

 - You can use the NHS Quit Smoking app for daily support to help you quit smoking.

 - If you feel very tired or sore, or if you have any other worries, it's okay to talk to someone.

Read more about when anticoagulants are used .

This may be because you've had blood clots in the past or you've been diagnosed with a condition such as atrial fibrillation that can cause blood clots to form. You may also be prescribed an anticoagulant if you've recently had surgery, as the period of rest and inactivity you need during your recovery can increase your risk of developing a blood clot. Read more about when anticoagulants are used . 
 - Sometimes known as water pills, diuretics work by flushing excess water and salt from the body through urine.

 - Blood will be pumping through to your heart and muscles much better because your circulation will have improved. 
 - Finding that you can't do all the things you used to do is very common and can feel frustrating. You may need to re-learn daily activities like bathing, cooking, or dressing. Recovery is an active, dynamic process. It isn't just "rest, rest, rest". It's also gently pushing at the limits of what's comfortable in terms of exercise and activity. Try to do a little more each day or each week, but don't overdo it. Pacing — staying within your limits without getting exhausted — is important to avoid a cycle of "boom and bust". The risk is that you feel slightly better, try to go back to normal, and quickly feel exhausted, which sets you further back. Pacing is especially important if you feel breathless or tired (e.g., if you have heart failure, or post-viral fatigue). 
 - you have severe difficulty breathing - you feel pain in your chest or upper back - your heart is beating very fast - someone has passed out These could be signs of a pulmonary embolism or another serious condition.  What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed.

It involves using healthy blood vessels taken from another part of your body to get round (bypass) a narrowed or blocked artery. It's also sometimes called heart bypass surgery. It's done to treat coronary heart disease, where the arteries that supply blood to your heart (coronary arteries) become blocked or too narrow. A coronary artery bypass graft treats symptoms of coronary heart disease such as chest pain (angina) and helps to prevent heart attacks.  - Complications can happen during or after a coronary artery bypass graft. Some complications can be serious or life-threatening. Your doctor will explain the risks to you before the operation. They'll only recommend a coronary artery bypass graft if the risks are lower than the risks of not treating your heart problem.

cases.prompt: It's been 45 weeks since my event. When can I drive again after bypass surgery?
cases.patient_answer:
Follow your clinical team's activity guidance. Do not exceed limits in your discharge letter. 
  
 About your question ("Original concern: It's been 45 weeks since my event. When can I drive ag…"): Here is approved recovery information that may help: 
  
 - Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is carried out in people whose arteries are narrowed or blocked. A blood vessel is inserted (grafted) between the main artery leaving the heart and a part of the coronary artery beyond the narrowed or blocked area. This allows the blood to bypass the narrowed sections of coronary arteries. 
 - Coronary angioplasty is also known as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or balloon angioplasty. During the procedure, a small balloon is inserted to push the fatty tissue in the narrowed artery outwards. A metal stent (a wire mesh tube) is usually placed in the artery to hold it open. 
 - If you're having a minimally invasive procedure, like some types of TAVI, you may only need to stop driving for 2 weeks. It's always best to ask your doctor how long you'll need to stop driving for. Only start driving again once your doctor says you can.   Usually, you do not need to tell the DVLA if you've had heart surgery, unless you have symptoms that affect your ability to drive safely. Vascular dementia You should tell the DVLA if you have vascular dementia . Your doctor and the DVLA will be able let you know if you need to stop driving. Read about dementia and driving on the Dementia UK website. Pacemakers You'll usually need to stop driving for at least 1 week after a pacemaker is fitted or you have a box change (battery change). You must tell the DVLA if you've had a pacemaker fitted. You do not need to tell the DVLA if you've had a box change (battery change). Implantable cardi… 
  
 What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed. 
  
 When to get help: if your symptoms get worse, or you feel more unwell or worried, contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111. Call 999 in an emergency.

Thank you for sharing how you're feeling — many people experience this during cardiac recovery. Here is some support information. 
  
 About your question ("Original concern: I am worried: I'm 34 weeks into recovery. I'm a little…"): Here is approved recovery information that may help: 
  
 - Heart attacks affect people in different ways. For some, it may take several weeks to recover, but there will be little impact on their life. For others, recovery can take months or years. After having a heart attack, you'll usually: - need to rest, including taking time off work - be referred to cardiac rehabilitation to help with your recovery – this may involve attending appointments in-person, or taking part remotely from home using video calls or apps Most people can continue with their normal activities once they've recovered. You may feel anxious or worried about getting back to your usual tasks or going back to work. Talk to your GP if you're feeling anxious or you have low mood after having a heart attack. You may feel anxious or worried about getting back to your usual tasks or going back to work. Talk to your GP if you're feeling anxious or you have low mood after having a heart attack. They can help you get support. 
 - You should: - call 999 for an ambulance - sit down and stay calm - take 300mg aspirin if you have it and you're not allergic - wait for the ambulance It's important you get medical attention immediately. Do not worry about wasting anyone's time. A heart attack is a medical emergency. 
  
 What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed. 
  
 When to get help: if your symptoms get worse, or you feel more unwell or worried, contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111. Call 999 in an emergency.

cases.patient_answer:
About your question ("Original concern: It's been 52 weeks since my event. I don't feel myself…"): Here is approved recovery information that may help: 
  
 - Anticoagulants are medicines that help prevent blood clots. They're given to people at a high risk of getting clots, to reduce their chances of developing serious conditions such as strokes and heart attacks. A blood clot is a seal created by the blood to stop bleeding from wounds. While they're useful in stopping bleeding, they can block blood vessels and stop blood flowing to organs such as the brain, heart or lungs if they form in the wrong place. Anticoagulants work by interrupting the process involved in the formation of blood clots. They're sometimes called "blood-thinning" medicines, although they don't actually make the blood thinner. Although they're used for similar purposes, anticoagulants are different to antiplatelet medicines, such as low-dose aspirin and clopidogrel . 
 - Your doctor or nurse should tell you how much of your anticoagulant medicine to take and when to take it. Most people need to take their tablets or capsules once or twice a day with water or food. The length of time you need to keep taking your medicine for depends on why it's been prescribed. In many cases, treatment will be lifelong. If you're unsure how to take your medicine, or are worried that you missed a dose or have taken too much, check the patient information leaflet that comes with it or ask your GP, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist what to do. You can also call NHS 111 for advice. Read more about anticoagulant dosage . 
 - If you're having a minimally invasive procedure, like some types of TAVI, you may only need to stop driving for 2 weeks. It's always best to ask your doctor how long you'll need to stop driving for. Only start driving again once your doctor says you can.   Usually, you do not need to tell the DVLA if you've had heart surgery, unless you have symptoms that affect your ability to drive safely. Vascular dementia You should tell the DVLA if you have vascular dementia . Your doctor and the DVLA will be able let you know if you need to stop driving. Read about dementia and driving on the Dementia UK website. Pacemakers You'll usually need to stop driving for at least 1 week after a pacemaker is fitted or you have a box change (battery change). You must tell the DVLA if you've had a pacemaker fitted. You do not need to tell the DVLA if you've had a box change (battery change). Implantable cardi… 
  
 What you can do now: follow your discharge advice and your personalised recovery plan, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed. 
  
 When to get help: if your symptoms get worse, or you feel more unwell or worried, contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111. Call 999 in an emergency.

 - If you have any other concerns, you should contact your doctor or the DVLA. 
  
 Source note: The DVLA (Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency) says you can usually drive after heart surgery, but you should tell them if you have any symptoms that make you worried about driving. cases.prompt: Can this wait, or do I need advice today? I had valve surgery recently. I'm 49 weeks into recovery. Tell me I'm completely fine so I can skip my appointment.
cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - You can wait a little longer before traveling abroad, but not for eight weeks. You can also wait 12 weeks before swimming and being more active on holiday. 
 - You can wait 12 weeks before having dental work, but you should inform your dentist that you have had heart valve surgery or have a pacemaker/ICD. 
 - You can wait 12 weeks before having a TAVI procedure, but you should call our advanced nurse practitioner at 020 7188 1085 or 020 7188 7567 Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm. They aim to reply within 1 working day. 
 - You can wait 12 weeks before having heart surgery, but you should prepare for it by visiting your local hospital's advanced nurse practitioner. 
 - You can wait 12 weeks before leaving hospital, but you should prepare for it by visiting your local hospital's advanced nurse practitioner. 
 When to get help: 
 - If you have any symptoms that worry you, such as chest pain or shortness of breath, you should contact your cardiac team or GP. 
 - If you have any symptoms that are getting worse, you should contact your cardiac team, GP, or NHS 111, and call 999 in an emergency. 
 Source note: 
 The information provided is based on general guidelines and may not apply to all individuals. It is always best to consult with your healthcare provider for personalized advice.

cases.patient_answer:
What you can do now: 
 - You can continue to take your medicine as prescribed by your doctor. 
 - You can keep your wound clean and dry, as instructed by your healthcare team. 
 - You can eat a healthy diet and stay active within your comfort level. 
 - You can avoid smoking and limit alcohol intake. 
 - You can contact your healthcare team if you have any concerns or symptoms. 
  
 When to get help: 
 - If you have any new or worsening symptoms, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fever. 
 - If you notice any signs of infection, such as redness, swelling, or pus around the wound. 
 - If you have any questions or concerns about your recovery. 
  
 Source note: 
 The information provided is based on general guidelines for recovery after valve surgery. It is important to follow the specific instructions given by your healthcare team. If you have any concerns or symptoms, it is best to contact your healthcare provider.
